![Blank five-step biography timeline with fields for date clue, event, page, and why it mattered](images/grade-04/ela/g04-ela-biography-evidence-timeline.png)

Fill the timeline from the source being read. Record the source and page before explaining why an event mattered; the blank organizer itself does not supply facts.

**Verified school reading:** P.S. 179's dated HMH Into Reading Module 1 list includes *Queen of Physics*, a biography of physicist Chien-Shiung Wu. The publisher and author describe the book as covering Wu's education and career, her beta-decay research, and barriers she faced as a Chinese American woman in science. Use the assigned copy from Sora or the school library for its actual text and illustrations; this guide does not reproduce the book. [NYC Reads Finder](https://curriculum-finder.vercel.app/); [publisher description](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/teresa-robeson/queen-of-physics/9781454932208/); [author's book page](https://teresarobeson.com/queen-of-physics).

**Accessible source reading:** the short reading below is a new plain-English paraphrase of facts in the National Park Service's biography of Wu. It is a companion source, not a passage from *Queen of Physics*. The questions and answers about this paragraph refer to the NPS source. [National Park Service biography](https://www.nps.gov/people/dr-chienshiung-wu.htm).

#### Reading: Chien-Shiung Wu follows the evidence

Chien-Shiung Wu was born near Shanghai, China, in 1912. As a child, she studied at a school her father had started. She later studied physics at a university in Shanghai. In 1936, she moved to the United States. She earned a PhD at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1940. During World War II, she worked at Columbia University on the Manhattan Project, including work with radiation detectors. After the war, she continued to study beta decay. In 1956, she carried out an experiment that tested an idea about parity in physics. In 1957, two other physicists received the Nobel Prize for related work; Wu did not receive it then. Later, Wu spoke against unfair treatment of women. In 1978, she received the first Wolf Prize in Physics.

This paraphrase follows the facts and sequence reported by the National Park Service. It does not replace the book or add page details from the school copy.

**Goal:** use dates and events to explain how a person's experiences shaped her path. Separate what a source says from what a reader infers.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute reading/writing work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read for facts | Read the paraphrase once. Circle names and dates; underline school, work, and award details. Read the matching assigned-book pages if available. | State which source a fact came from; do not blend facts from two sources without noting both. |
| 2 — Build a timeline | Put five events in order. Add a source label and page number for book facts; cite “NPS biography” for companion-reading facts. | Events are in time order and every fact has a source marker. |
| 3 — Cause, choice, and result | Choose one move or career change. Write what happened before it, the change, and what the source says happened after. Mark any “because” statement as an inference unless the source states the reason. | Tell the difference between event order and a proven cause. |
| 4 — Compare sources and theme | Compare how the NPS biography and assigned book present Wu. Find one fact both support and one detail that appears in only one source. Draft a theme claim with two pieces of evidence. | Evidence is accurately attributed; a theme is a lesson or idea, not just a topic word. |
| 5 — Write and revise | Write 2–3 paragraphs about a real time the learner practiced, solved a hard problem, or helped someone. Include the situation, action, response, and ending. Revise for order, detail, and complete sentences. | The story is true to the writer's experience and has a clear sequence; it need not resemble Wu's life. |

#### Practice set — new questions, not school or NYSED test questions

Answer 1–8 from the short NPS-based reading above. Answer 9–12 from the assigned book if available, with page evidence; if it is not available, use another teacher-approved biography and name that source.

1. Where and when was Wu born?
2. Name one place where Wu studied and one subject she studied.
3. What did she earn at the University of California, Berkeley, and in what year?
4. What work did the passage say she did during World War II?
5. What did she continue to study after the war?
6. What happened in 1957, and what important fact about Wu does the passage add?
7. Put these in time order: the 1956 experiment, her move to the United States, her 1940 PhD.
8. Does the passage say why Wu moved to the United States? Use the text to explain your answer.
9. From the book, record one challenge or barrier and the page where it appears.
10. From the book, record what Wu did in response to one challenge; cite the page.
11. Write one theme claim about learning, evidence, or fairness. Give two events from the book or clearly identified sources that support it.
12. Write a true personal narrative with a beginning, important event, response, and ending. Underline the sentence that shows the turning point.

#### Checked answer and review guide

2. She studied at a **university in Shanghai** and studied **physics**. She later studied at UC Berkeley too.
3. A **PhD in 1940**.
4. She worked at **Columbia University on the Manhattan Project**, including work with radiation detectors.
5. **Beta decay.**
6. Two other physicists received the **Nobel Prize for related work**; the passage says Wu **did not receive it then**.
7. **Move to the United States (1936), PhD (1940), 1956 experiment.**
8. **No reason is given** in this short reading. Do not guess a reason; locate a source that states it if you want to answer why.
9–10. Answers depend on the assigned book or named alternate reading. Accept only a challenge/response shown in that source, with a page or section reference.
11. Answers vary. A strong answer states one theme and connects two separate, accurate events to it. A theme must say something about the topic, not only name it.
12. Answers vary. The narrative must describe the student's real experience, keep the events in order, and mark a clear moment when something changed.

**Mastery check:** the learner orders events by dates, attributes facts to a source, uses accurate evidence, avoids inventing a cause, and writes a true personal narrative with a clear sequence.

English.title: Module 1 companion week: Jella Lepman and a library for children
English.subject: English
English.contentMarkdown:
**School connection:** the dated P.S. 179 Grade 4 HMH Module 1 record lists *Jella Lepman and Her Library of Dreams*. This guide cannot verify the book's full text or the teacher's assigned pages. The study below is a separate source-based companion using the International Youth Library's own history page. It must not be presented as an HMH excerpt or a confirmed classroom assignment. [P.S. 179 Module 1 source record and book link](https://soraapp.com/library/nycschools/search/query-jella/titles/310229/10980615) · [International Youth Library: History](https://www.ijb.de/en/about-us/history).

#### Read: books connect children after war

Jella Lepman was a Jewish children's author and journalist. After living in exile in Britain, she returned to Germany after World War II to work on cultural and learning projects for women and children in the American-occupied zone. The International Youth Library's history says that many children and teenagers had been hurt by the war and had grown up under Nazi rule. Lepman believed books from many countries could help children learn about one another.

She asked publishers in different countries to donate children's books. The library's history reports that she gathered 4,000 books from 14 countries. In July 1946, people could see those books at an international children's literature exhibition in a Munich art museum. That exhibit helped lead to the idea of a permanent library. It took about three more years to secure money and work through the steps needed to open it.

The International Youth Library opened to the public on September 14, 1949, in a villa in Munich. The history says it opened with about 8,000 books. Children could choose books, read stories and comics from other countries, and talk about new books. The library also offered activities such as a youth theater group, language classes, a painting workshop, and a children's Model United Nations. The library describes these activities as ways to help children meet ideas and people from other places. This source is the library's own history; it supports facts about the institution, but it does not tell us what every child who visited thought or felt.

**Words to know:** *exile* — living away from one's home country, often because it is not safe to stay; *publisher* — a person or company that prepares books to be shared with readers; *exhibition* — a public show of objects or works; *permanent* — meant to continue, not just happen for a short time; *institution* — an organization created for a purpose; *inference* — an idea a reader draws from facts, but that the source may not state directly.

#### Five-session study plan — 50–60 minutes each

| Session | Read, investigate, and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Identify the source and the person | Read the passage, then open the library history. Mark each fact about Lepman, the exhibition, and the library. Record the source title and the date of the page if it is shown. | A fact chart with three columns: person, events, source clue. |
| 2 — Build a dated timeline | Use the blank biography timeline below. Place only the events and dates the source gives: the July 1946 exhibition and September 14, 1949 opening. Put the book gathering before the exhibition only as the source describes it; do not invent a day or month. | A two-date timeline with one source clue next to each event and a note that the book gathering has no exact date in this account. |
| 3 — Follow an idea into action | Make a chain: Lepman wanted children to encounter books from other countries → she asked publishers for donations → an exhibition showed the books → a permanent library opened. Mark which links the source states and which sentence explains the chain in your own words. | A cause-and-action chain with every fact attributed to the library history. |
| 4 — Compare the numbers carefully | Compare 4,000 books from 14 countries in the collection for the exhibition with about 8,000 books when the library opened. Explain why these are two counts at two different times. The source does not say that the exact same books stayed or that the collection doubled in a particular way. | A number comparison using dates, “about” where needed, and a sentence naming what the source does not prove. |
| 5 — Explain experience and identity | Write a short biography paragraph: who Lepman was, one experience named by the source, one action she took, and one supported idea about why the library mattered. End by saying what you would still need to read in the HMH book to describe its scenes or illustrations. | A paragraph with at least three source facts, a clear inference label, and no invented book details. |

#### Source-based practice — new questions for this guide

1. What two kinds of work does the library history name for Jella Lepman?
2. Where had Lepman lived before returning to Germany?
3. What kind of work did she return to do in the American-occupied zone?
4. How many children's books did the history say she gathered, and from how many countries?
5. What happened to those books in Munich in July 1946?
6. What idea grew from the exhibition?
7. On what date did the International Youth Library open to the public?
8. About how many books did it have when it opened?
9. Name two activities the library offered besides choosing and reading books.
10. Put these in time order: the library opened; the book exhibition took place; Lepman asked publishers for books.
11. Why is “about 8,000” more careful than writing “exactly 8,000”?
12. Does this history tell us what every child thought about the library? What does it tell us instead?
13. Is “books from different countries could help children learn about one another” a direct fact or an inference from Lepman's goal and the library's activities? Explain.
14. What is one difference between the 1946 book count and the 1949 book count? Give the dates and keep the two counts separate.
15. Write a four-sentence biography summary that includes one fact about Lepman's identity, one dated event, one action, and one idea the source supports.

#### Checked answer guide

1. Children's author and journalist. 2. Britain; the source says she returned from British exile. 3. Cultural and educational work for women and children. 4. 4,000 books from 14 countries. 5. They were shown at an international children's literature exhibition in a Munich art museum. 6. The idea of establishing a permanent international children's library. 7. September 14, 1949. 8. About 8,000 books. 9. Accept two named activities: youth theater, language courses, a painting workshop, author talks/book discussions, or the children's Model UN. 10. Lepman asked publishers for books → the exhibition took place in July 1946 → the library opened in 1949. 11. The library history says “about” 8,000, so the source gives an approximate count. 12. No; it describes the collection, opening, and activities, but does not report every visitor's thoughts. 13. It is an inference. The source reports Lepman's goal and the library's activities; the sentence explains how they may connect. 14. The source reports 4,000 books from 14 countries for the exhibition and about 8,000 books when the library opened three years later. These are counts at different points, not a precise record of which books were added or removed. 15. Check that the identity, date, and action match the source, and that the idea is supported and labeled as an inference. Wording may differ.

**Visual:** Reuse the blank [Grade 4 biography evidence timeline](images/grade-04/ela/g04-ela-biography-evidence-timeline.png). It has no names or dates printed in it, so it can organize this source as well as the Queen of Physics reading. Keep the source date beside each event. Do not fill in an exact date for the book gathering: the library history does not give one.

**Source limit:** These facts are paraphrased from the International Youth Library's institutional history. For the HMH book's own scenes, wording, and art, use the licensed book. The library's history supports its own dates and collection figures; it is not a first-person account by Lepman or a report from every child who visited.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: New York State geography and map evidence
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
![Blank source-analysis organizer for the source type, creator, date, map or document, observation, inference, and follow-up checks](images/grade-04/social-studies/g04-social-source-analysis-organizer.png)

Use the organizer to record the map's title, date, type, what it shows, and what still needs another source.

**Verified course content:** NYC Passport Grade 4 is **New York State and Local History**. Its first unit is **The Geography of New York State**; the course description says students study geography, history, economics, government, and local connections. [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade). The public page links Unit 1 guides and workbooks, but access to the student materials may require an NYCPS login. A separate NYCDOE program list for 2019–20 names these Unit 1 trade books: *Me on the Map* by Joan Sweeney, *New York's Land and Natural Resources* by Daniel R. Faust, and *River of Dreams: The Story of the Hudson River* by Hudson Talbott. That older list documents curriculum materials; it does not prove P.S. 179 currently assigns those books. [NYCDOE Grade 4 curriculum list (2019–20)](https://infohub.nyced.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/grade-4-social-studies-curriculum.pdf).

**Source-backed lesson content:** the New York State Grade 4 framework says students use physical and thematic maps to explore the state's geography. Its examples include mountains, plateaus, rivers, lakes, the Atlantic Ocean, and Long Island Sound. It also calls for a political map showing the state capital, major cities, boundaries, and the student's own community; students compare climate and vegetation maps with a physical map. These are framework expectations, not proof of P.S. 179's week-by-week sequence. [NYS K–8 Social Studies Framework, Grade 4 Key Idea 4.1](https://www.nysed.gov/common/nysed/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf).

#### Learn it in plain English

Maps are tools. A **physical map** shows natural features such as mountains, rivers, and lakes. A **political map** shows boundaries and places governed as cities, states, or countries. A **thematic map** focuses on one topic, such as climate or vegetation. The title, date, legend (key), labels, compass directions, and scale help a reader understand what is shown. One map cannot answer every question.

Start with the map's title and date. Use the legend to learn what colors and symbols mean. Use the compass rose or north arrow for direction. If the map has a scale, use it to estimate distance; do not treat the drawing's visual size as the real distance. Record what is visible before explaining why it may matter.

Example source note: “The map labels the Hudson River and shows it reaching the New York City area.” That is an **observation** if the chosen map visibly shows those labels and features. “The river helped people travel or move goods” is an **inference** that needs another historical or geographic source before it can be stated as a fact about a specific community. On an old map, names and boundaries describe what the mapmaker recorded at that time; check a current map for present-day facts.

#### Source reading: follow the Mohawk River across New York

The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) describes the Mohawk as the largest tributary of the Hudson River. The Mohawk's headwaters are between the southwestern Adirondack Mountains and the eastern edge of the Tug Hill Plateau. The river flows south toward Rome, turns east, and travels about **140 miles** before joining the Hudson at Cohoes. NYSDEC also says the river's basin covers about **3,460 square miles**, roughly one quarter of the Hudson River drainage area. [NYSDEC, Mohawk River Watershed](https://dec.ny.gov/nature/waterbodies/watersheds/management/mohawk-river-watershed).

A **tributary** is a river or stream that flows into a larger river. **Headwaters** are the upper areas where a river begins. A **watershed** or **basin** is land where water drains toward the same river or water system. **Land use** means how people use land, such as for farms, homes, or forests. A **floodplain** is low, fairly flat land beside a river; it can flood. On a map, a river line can help a reader follow direction, but the line alone does not explain why a city grew or what people did there. NYSDEC also notes that the Mohawk River route serves the Erie (Barge) Canal. That is evidence of a connection between a river and a human-made water route; more history sources are needed to explain how or why it was built.

NYSDEC describes land-use patterns in the basin. Forest cover dominates in the Adirondack part of the basin and around Schoharie Creek. Farming is more common near the main Mohawk River in the fertile floodplain. Homes, businesses, and industries are concentrated mostly in population centers along the river and canal. This source describes where these land uses occur; it does not prove that the river alone caused farms or towns to be there. [NYSDEC, Mohawk River Watershed](https://dec.ny.gov/nature/waterbodies/watersheds/management/mohawk-river-watershed).

**Map visual:** Open NYSDEC's [Mohawk River/Barge Canal map (PDF)](https://dec.ny.gov/sites/default/files/2024-04/mohawkriverbargecanal.pdf) beside the blank source organizer above. It maps the Mohawk corridor from Rome east toward Waterford, with major streams, county borders, and a distance scale. Trace the river toward Cohoes and the Hudson; copy labels only when the map shows them. Use NYSDEC's [New York State watershed map](https://dec.ny.gov/nature/waterbodies/watersheds) to see how the Mohawk basin fits among the state's larger drainage basins. The 1902 historical map elsewhere in this file can support a dated comparison, but it is not a current base map.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Map purpose and parts | Use a current state map and the dated 1902 map. For each, record title, date, map type, key/legend, direction marker, and scale if shown. List two visible details before making an inference. | State which question each map can answer and one question it cannot answer. |
| 2 — Physical features and a river path | On a current physical map, locate examples named in the NYS framework: mountains, plateaus, rivers, lakes, the Atlantic Ocean, and Long Island Sound. Then use the NYSDEC Mohawk map to trace headwaters, Rome, Cohoes, and the Hudson. Copy map labels exactly. | Name which features are land and water; trace the Mohawk's south-then-east route using map evidence. |
| 3 — Political map and place | On a current political map, locate the state capital, major cities shown by that source, state borders, and the student's own community. Locate Rome and Cohoes if the map labels them. Use north/south/east/west to compare locations. | The explanation names the map and direction evidence used. |
| 4 — Compare map layers and source text | Compare the Mohawk watershed map with a physical map. Record one fact the DEC text states and one pattern visible on each map. Write a cautious question about a possible relationship; do not claim that the map proves a cause. | Label text facts, map observations, and inferences separately. |
| 5 — Make a source-based map card | Choose the Mohawk River or another visible feature. Complete the organizer: title/date, three observations, one inference labeled as an inference, and one fact that needs another source. If comparing with the 1902 map, keep its date beside every claim. | The card keeps historical evidence dated and does not present it as current. |

#### Practice set — new map-reading drills, not school or NYSED test questions

For questions 1–9, use a current teacher-approved New York State map. Answers that depend on a map must match the map actually used.

1. What map parts tell you the topic, symbol meanings, and direction?
2. Which map is a better first choice for locating rivers and mountains: physical or political? Why?
3. Which map is a better first choice for locating state borders and a capital city? Why?
4. The NYS framework names mountains, plateaus, rivers, lakes, the Atlantic Ocean, and Long Island Sound as features students locate. Sort these into land and water features.
5. Find the state capital on the current political map. Copy the label and describe its direction from your community, using the map.
6. Find one major river label on the physical map. Write exactly what the map shows about where it is; do not add an unshown cause or history.
7. A climate map is shaded by region. What must you read before saying what one color means?
8. A 1902 map and a current map show different boundary lines. Which map should answer a question about present-day boundaries? What can the 1902 map answer?
9. Write two source notes: one visible observation and one inference that would need another source.
10. Why should a reader compare physical and vegetation maps instead of assuming a land feature caused a plant pattern?
11. A map has no scale. Can you use it to calculate an exact travel distance? Explain.
12. Create a map card with a title, date, legend, one land feature, one water feature, and a note about what your map does not show. Use a real current map and cite its title/source.
13. According to NYSDEC, which river is the Mohawk's largest tributary?
14. Between which two land regions are the Mohawk headwaters located?
15. Describe the route NYSDEC gives from the headwaters to the Hudson. Include the southward and eastward turns.
16. About how long is the Mohawk River, and where does it join the Hudson?
17. About how large is the Mohawk River basin? About what fraction of the Hudson River drainage area does NYSDEC say it covers?
18. What is a tributary? Use the Mohawk and Hudson to explain.
19. What does NYSDEC say the Mohawk River route also serves?
20. Write one direct fact from the NYSDEC text and one question that the text/map does not answer. Label them “source fact” and “open question.”
21. Where does NYSDEC say forest cover dominates in the Mohawk River Basin?
22. Where does NYSDEC say agriculture is more common?
23. Where are homes, businesses, and industries mostly concentrated, according to NYSDEC?
24. Does the source prove that the river alone caused these land-use patterns? Explain.

#### Checked answer and review guide

1. The **title** gives the topic, the **legend/key** explains symbols, and the **compass rose/north arrow** gives direction. Accept equivalent map labels.
2. A **physical map**, because it focuses on natural land and water features.
3. A **political map**, because it focuses on boundaries, cities, and government locations.
4. Land: **mountains, plateaus**. Water: **rivers, lakes, Atlantic Ocean, Long Island Sound**.
5. Answers depend on the current map and the learner's community. Credit the exact capital label and a direction supported by the map; do not provide a memorized direction without checking.
6. Answers depend on the map. The location statement must match its river label and visible path; mark anything beyond the map as a question or inference.
7. Read the map's **legend/key**; colors can mean different things on different maps.
8. Use the **current map** for present-day boundaries. Use the 1902 map only to study what was shown at that date.
9. Example observation: “The map labels ____.” Example inference: “This location may affect ____.” The inference must be marked and supported by an added source before it is treated as fact.
10. The maps show different information. Comparing them can reveal patterns to investigate, but a pattern alone does not prove cause.
11. **No**, not exactly. Without a scale or another distance source, the drawing does not tell the exact ground distance.
12. Answers depend on the selected map. Check the source title/date, accurate copied labels, clear legend, and honest limit statement.
13. **The Hudson River.**
14. **Between the southwestern Adirondack Mountains and the eastern edge of the Tug Hill Plateau.**
15. It flows **south toward Rome**, turns **east**, then continues to the Hudson at Cohoes. Accept close wording that preserves the directions and places.
16. **About 140 miles; it joins the Hudson at Cohoes.**
17. **About 3,460 square miles; roughly one quarter** of the Hudson River drainage area.
18. A tributary is a river or stream that flows into a larger river. The Mohawk is a tributary because it joins the Hudson.
19. **The Erie (Barge) Canal.**
20. Answers vary. The source fact must match NYSDEC; the open question must not be filled with an unsupported guess. Example fact: “NYSDEC says the Mohawk joins the Hudson at Cohoes.” Example open question: “How did the canal change travel for people living near the river?”
21. In the **Adirondack part of the basin and around the Schoharie Creek watershed**.
22. Near the **main Mohawk River, in the fertile floodplain**.
23. Mostly in **population centers along the main river and barge canal**.
24. **No.** NYSDEC reports where these land uses occur; another source would be needed to explain all the causes.

**Mastery check:** the learner chooses a map that fits the question, reads its title and legend, cites visible map evidence, uses direction or scale only when shown, and separates observation from inference.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Onondaga Nation, wampum, and records of agreement
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** NYC Passport Grade 4 Unit 2 is **Native Americans: First Inhabitants of New York State**. This week studies one living Haudenosaunee nation, the Onondaga Nation, through its own public explanations of wampum and a dated first-person account, alongside a New York State Archives finding aid. It is a source-based supplement, not evidence that P.S. 179 assigned this specific case study or sequence. One Onondaga example must not stand for all Native nations. [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade).

**Reading — student-friendly paraphrase of the sources:**

The Onondaga Nation is a current nation in New York State, south of Syracuse. The Nation says it is one member of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, which has six nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and Tuscarora. The Nation explains that **wampum** is important in Haudenosaunee life. Wampum beads are made from shell; the beads can be white or purple and can be woven into strings and belts. The Nation says these records help carry messages, remember events and agreements, and take part in ceremonies. Its source describes wampum as living history, not only as decoration.

The Onondaga Nation's page about the **Hiawatha Belt** explains that the belt tells a story about five nations joining in peace: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca. It describes a longhouse as a way to picture the nations together while each nation has its own council fire. The same page says Clan Mothers have authority to replace leaders. These are the Nation's explanations of its own traditions. The belt page describes five nations in the founding story; the Nation's current “About Us” page lists six nations, including Tuscarora. Keep those time and source details clear.

Two sources describe what happened when wampum belts returned to Onondaga in 1989. Chief Irving Powless Jr.'s account, published by the Onondaga Nation and dated October 21, 1989, describes the return ceremony and says he took part in signing an agreement. A New York State Archives finding aid summarizes a historical bill of sale and a Council record, says the bill of sale was signed by Onondaga sachems and chiefs, and explains that a 1971 law allowed the belts to be returned under a preservation condition. The Archives says the belts were returned in 1989. The finding aid describes archived documents; it is not the original bill of sale itself. The original document has access restrictions. These sources emphasize different parts of the history, so a careful reader names the source and does not claim that a short summary answers every question about consent, custody, or the full agreement.

**Key words:** **wampum** is shell beads woven into strings or belts and used in ways described by Haudenosaunee sources; a **belt** is an object that can carry a record or message; a **Confederacy** is an alliance of nations; a **Clan Mother** is a woman with an important leadership role in the Haudenosaunee government described by the Nation; a **finding aid** is an archive's guide to records in a collection; **first-person account** is a record written by someone who took part in or witnessed an event.

**Visuals:** The Onondaga Nation page shows a [Hiawatha Belt image](https://www.onondaganation.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Hiawatha-Belt-300x164.jpg) and explains how the Nation reads it. Use the existing [Grade 4 source-analysis organizer](images/grade-04/social-studies/g04-social-source-analysis-organizer.png) to note who created each source, what it says, and what it does not answer. Credit the belt image to the Onondaga Nation and link its [Hiawatha Belt explanation](https://www.onondaganation.org/culture/wampum/hiawatha-belt/). No generated image is needed for this week.

**Five sessions, about 45–60 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: the Battle of Brooklyn — read a 1776 map
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** NYC Passport Grade 4 Unit 3 is **Colonial and Revolutionary Periods**. The public course page says Grade 4 studies New York State and local communities over time. This Brooklyn-area case study uses a contemporary manuscript map and later National Park Service explanations; it is a supplement, not confirmation that P.S. 179 follows this lesson or calendar. [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade).

**Reading — student-friendly paraphrase of the sources:**

In August 1776, British and Continental Army forces fought on Long Island in what is now Brooklyn. The Library of Congress catalog calls the event the Battle of Long Island; the National Park Service calls it the Battle of Brooklyn. These are two names for this battle. The Library of Congress holds a large manuscript map titled as a map of British and American troop positions in the New York City region during August and September 1776. Its catalog dates it approximately to 1776. A manuscript map from that period is a primary source: it is evidence made close to the events. The mapmaker is not named in the catalog information. A map is still a person's selection of places and marks; it does not show every person's experience or explain each decision.

The National Park Service says that the first shots were fired on August 26. A second NPS article places the main British attack early on August 27. These details can fit together: the first shots and the main fighting need not have happened on the same day. NPS says that British and allied troops trapped Continental Army soldiers in Brooklyn Heights, with the East River behind them. Washington ordered a nighttime evacuation across the river to Manhattan. The soldiers left campfires burning and kept quiet; fog covered the final part of the crossing. The NPS account says the troops reached Manhattan by 7 a.m. The Continental Army had retreated, and British forces held New York City for the rest of the war, until 1783.

Another NPS account describes the Maryland and Delaware soldiers who stayed behind near the Old Stone House in Brooklyn to help other soldiers escape. It reports that 256 Maryland and Delaware soldiers were killed near the house and more were captured. The NPS article points out that “Maryland 400” is an incomplete name for this group because Delaware soldiers were also there. Treat that number as the NPS report, and remember that it describes deaths in a battle, not a score or a game.

**Key words:** **manuscript map** is a hand-drawn map; **primary source** is an item made during or close to the time being studied; **secondary source** explains the past later, using evidence; **Continental Army** was the army formed by the colonies; **retreat** is moving away from a battle or danger; a **rear guard** is a group that stays behind to protect others as they leave.

**Visual sources:** Open the [Library of Congress manuscript map](https://www.loc.gov/item/2003630407/) and use the viewer to zoom in. The LOC catalog identifies it as a map of troop positions in the New York City region during the Battle of Long Island and gives its date as approximately 1776. The LOC says its digitized Geography and Map Division material is free to use and reuse unless a rights advisory says otherwise; credit the Library of Congress. Use the existing [Grade 4 source-analysis organizer](images/grade-04/social-studies/g04-social-source-analysis-organizer.png) to record what the map shows and what the later NPS sources explain.

![An 1874 engraving of the Battle of Long Island, made from a painting by Alonzo Chappel; this is a later depiction, not an image made during the 1776 battle](https://www.nps.gov/gois/learn/historyculture/images/revolutionary-war1_1.jpg?autorotate=false&maxwidth=650)

**Image caption:** The NPS identifies this as an 1874 engraving based on a painting by Alonzo Chappel, with the image from the National Archives and Records Administration. It was made nearly a century after the battle, so use it as a later artist's depiction, not eyewitness evidence. The LOC manuscript map is the closer-to-event visual source.

**Five sessions, about 45–60 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Name and locate the event | Read the NYC Grade 4 Unit 3 title. On a modern New York map, locate Brooklyn, Manhattan, and the East River. Read the LOC catalog title and dates before opening the manuscript map. | Write the two names used for the battle and explain why a 1776 map title might say “Long Island” where a modern reader expects “Brooklyn.” Keep the date attached to each map. |
| 2 — Read the primary map | Open the LOC map. Find its title, date, legend or labels, water, and troop positions. Zoom rather than guessing at crowded details. | Record three map observations, one location question, and one thing that the map cannot show about the people in the battle. Mark each as “map evidence” or “question.” |
| 3 — Build a sourced timeline | Read the NPS Battle of Brooklyn page and the Maryland 400 account. Put the first shots, main attack, retreat, and arrival in Manhattan in order. | Make a four-event timeline. Note the NPS distinction between first shots on August 26 and the main attack on August 27. Cite the page beside each date. |
| 4 — Study the retreat and its human cost | Trace the East River crossing on a current map. Read the NPS account of the rear guard near the Old Stone House. | Write how the rear guard helped the retreat, then summarize the loss of life using NPS's wording. Note why “Maryland and Delaware 400” is more exact than “Maryland 400.” |
| 5 — Compare evidence and write | Compare the 1776 troop-position map with the later NPS explanations. Answer: “What can the map show about the battle, and what must we learn from another source?” | Write one paragraph with two map observations, two NPS facts, one source limit, and one question still unanswered. Don't describe the retreat as a victory; say who held New York City afterward. |

**Independent practice — guide-written questions, not copied from a school workbook:**

1. What is the title of NYC Passport Grade 4 Unit 3?
2. What two names do the Library of Congress and NPS use for the same battle?
3. Why can the LOC manuscript map be used as a primary source?
4. What does the map's approximate date, “[1776?],” tell a careful reader?
5. What kind of information does the LOC catalog say the map contains?
6. Name two things a troop-position map cannot prove by itself.
7. According to NPS, when were the first shots fired?
8. When does the second NPS article place the main attack?
9. Why are those dates not automatically a contradiction?
10. What river was behind the Continental Army at Brooklyn Heights?
11. What did Washington order the Continental Army to do?
12. Name one action the soldiers took to hide the nighttime evacuation.
13. By what time does the NPS article say the army reached Manhattan?
14. Who held New York City after the battle, and until what year?
15. What did the Maryland and Delaware rear guard do near the Old Stone House?
16. According to NPS, how many Maryland and Delaware soldiers were killed near the Old Stone House?
17. Why does NPS say “Maryland and Delaware 400” is more exact than “Maryland 400”?
18. Which source is primary for the troop positions: the 1776 manuscript map or the NPS article written later? Explain.
19. Give one fact the map supports and one question it cannot answer without another source.
20. Write four sentences explaining why the retreat mattered. Include one NPS fact, one map observation, and what happened to New York City afterward.

**Checked answers:** 1) **Colonial and Revolutionary Periods.** 2) The Library of Congress uses **Battle of Long Island**; NPS uses **Battle of Brooklyn**. 3) It is a manuscript map dated approximately to the time of the battle. 4) The catalog gives an approximate date, not a fully certain exact day or month. 5) British and American troop positions in the New York City region during August–September 1776. 6) Answers vary; it cannot by itself explain a person's thoughts, prove every soldier's action, or tell why a commander made a choice. 7) August 26, 1776. 8) Early on August 27, 1776. 9) The sources distinguish first shots from the main attack. 10) The East River. 11) Evacuate/retreat across the river to Manhattan. 12) They left campfires burning, muffled wagon wheels, or stayed quiet; any one supported detail. 13) By 7 a.m. 14) British forces held the city until 1783. 15) They stayed behind in a rear guard and fought near the Old Stone House so other Continental Army soldiers could escape. 16) The NPS article reports 256. 17) The group included Delaware soldiers as well as Maryland soldiers. 18) The 1776 manuscript map is primary because it was made close to the event; the later NPS article is secondary. 19) Answers vary. A map fact must match a visible label or mark; the question must be something the map does not show. 20) Check for a sourced map observation, a correct NPS fact, the retreat across the East River, and the fact that Britain held New York City until 1783. Accept clear, different wording.

**Source and perspective notes:** The [Library of Congress item record](https://www.loc.gov/item/2003630407/) provides the map title, approximate date, and rights information; the map itself is the primary source. The [NPS Battle of Brooklyn page](https://www.nps.gov/gois/learn/historyculture/battle-of-brooklyn.htm) and [NPS Maryland 400 article](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/the-maryland-400.htm) are later historical accounts. The casualty count is attributed to the Maryland 400 article. The LOC item page returned 403 to the research fetcher, so reopen the map link in a regular browser before publishing. These selected U.S. sources do not show every civilian, Loyalist, British, or other participant's perspective. They provide one local case study; they do not replace the full NYC Passport Unit 3 materials.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: who does what? Federal, New York State, and NYC government
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** The NYC Social Studies and Civics Hub lists Grade 4 Unit 4 as **Freedom and the New Nation: Federal, State, and Local Government**. This week follows that published topic with current public examples a Brooklyn student can locate. It is a source-based supplement; it does not prove the exact lesson order or teacher materials at P.S. 179. [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade).

**Learn it in plain English:**

People in the United States are served by more than one level of government. The **federal government** serves the whole country. **New York State government** serves people across New York State. **New York City government** makes and carries out decisions for the city. These levels have different jobs, but a real issue can involve more than one level. A useful first step is to look for the official office that says it handles the task, then read its directions.

The federal Constitution divides the federal government into three branches. **Congress** is the legislative branch: it makes federal laws. The **president and executive branch** carry out federal laws. The **federal courts** hear cases and explain how laws apply. A branch has a job in the federal government; it is not the same thing as a level of government.

New York State also has a legislature with two parts, the **Senate** and **Assembly**, and a governor who leads the state's executive branch. Courts are part of the state government too. New York's official Senate explanation describes these branches. At the city level, New York City's elected **Mayor** leads the city government and oversees city services. The **City Council**, with 51 elected members, makes local laws and approves the city budget. City agencies carry out services. The offices and services named here are examples, not a complete list of everything each government does.

Here are three real starting points for public tasks:

| Student question | Official office that gives the instructions | Level to start with | Evidence to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where can a person find instructions to apply for a U.S. passport? | U.S. Department of State, Passport Services | Federal | The page is on the State Department's official travel site. |
| Where can a New York resident find driver-license renewal instructions? | New York State Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) | State | NY DMV's page gives New York license-renewal steps. |
| Where can a Brooklyn household check its trash and recycling collection schedule? | NYC Department of Sanitation (DSNY), through NYC311 | City | NYC311 directs residents to DSNY service and collection-day information. |

These examples teach how to find the responsible office; they are not legal advice or rules for every situation. A passport is a federal service, while driver licensing is handled by New York State. For city trash collection, NYC's own service page is the right place to begin. If a problem crosses levels, follow the instructions of the agency that handles the specific service.

**Key words:** **government** is the system people use to make and carry out public decisions; **federal** means serving the United States as a whole; **state** means serving one state; **local** means serving a smaller area, such as a city; **branch** is one part of a government with a particular job; **legislative** means connected to making laws; **executive** means connected to carrying out laws and running services; **judicial** means connected to courts and legal cases; **agency** is an office that carries out public work; **evidence** is information that supports an answer.

**A source-reading habit:** A page's web address, heading, and “About” or contact information help identify who published it. Read the actual instruction, not only the logo. Write down (1) the office, (2) the task it says it handles, and (3) the words on the page that support your conclusion. Do not send a real request, share personal information, or submit a form for this practice.

**Five study sessions — about 50–65 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Sort the levels | Read the NYC Unit 4 title and the plain-English reading. Use the passport, NY DMV, and NYC sanitation examples. For each, circle the office name and underline the level clue. | Make three labeled boxes—Federal, New York State, NYC. Put each example in one box and copy one clue from the source that supports the choice. Add a fourth card marked “Need more information” for any example whose publisher or service is unclear. |
| 2 — Learn the branches | Read the USAGov page. Draw three boxes for Congress, President/executive branch, and federal courts. Add “makes laws,” “carries out laws,” and “hears cases/interprets laws” beside the matching box. Then compare this with the New York State Senate's branch explanation. | Write one sentence explaining why “federal” names a level and “legislative” names a branch job. Draw arrows only when a source supports the connection; do not assume that every government office has the same exact structure. |
| 3 — Look closely at city government | Read NYC's official “Your Government” page or, if it is unavailable, open NYC Council's official site and NYC311's sanitation page. Find the Mayor, City Council, and a city agency. Record one job for each from the page. | Complete: “The Mayor ___”; “The Council ___”; “DSNY/NYC311 helps residents ___.” Put the URL next to each fact. If a page is blocked, record “could not verify today” instead of guessing. |
| 4 — Match a question to a source | Reopen the three service examples and read the specific instructions. Practice asking, “Which office published this? What task does it describe? Which government level does that office belong to?” | Create three source cards with publisher, service, level, and one exact short phrase or page heading as evidence. Use no names, addresses, license numbers, or other personal details. |
| 5 — Explain and check | Review your boxes, branch diagram, and source cards. Complete the practice set below. Then teach a family member how to distinguish level from branch using one example of each. | Write a short answer: “A New York City resident needs to check the trash collection schedule. Which public source should they start with, and what evidence supports that choice? How is that different from asking which branch makes federal laws?” |

**Visual organizer:**

```text

United States — federal                   Congress — makes federal laws
New York — state                          President/executive — carries out laws
New York City — local                     Federal courts — hear cases and apply law

passport -> U.S. Department of State      Who makes federal laws? -> Congress
driver license -> NY DMV                  (A branch is a job within a level.)
trash schedule -> NYC311 / DSNY
```

Draw this in the existing [Grade 4 source-analysis organizer](images/grade-04/social-studies/g04-social-source-analysis-organizer.png), or copy it into a notebook. No new picture is needed for this lesson; the visual's purpose is to keep **level** and **branch** from getting mixed up.

**Practice — guide-written questions, not copied from a school workbook:**

1. What is the published title of NYC Grade 4 Unit 4?
2. Which level of government serves the United States as a whole?
3. Which level serves people across New York State?
4. Which level is the New York City government?
5. Is “federal” a government level or a branch job?
6. Is “legislative” a government level or a branch job?
7. Name the three branches of the federal government.
8. Which federal branch makes laws?
9. Which branch carries out federal laws?
10. What work do federal courts do in the three-branch explanation?
11. Which two elected parts make up New York State's legislature?
12. Which New York State leader heads the executive branch?
13. NYC's public page says the Mayor oversees city services. Is the Mayor part of the federal, state, or city level?
14. How many elected members does the NYC Council have, according to the city page used in this guide?
15. Name one job the NYC Council page says the Council does.
16. A person needs U.S. passport application instructions. Which official office is the source in this guide, and at what level?
17. A New York resident needs driver-license renewal instructions. Which office's page should they start with?
18. A Brooklyn household wants its trash collection day. Which public service source should it check first?
19. Why is “Congress is federal” not the same kind of answer as “Congress is legislative”?
20. A page has a government-looking logo but does not say it handles the problem. What should a careful reader do before trusting it?

**Checked answers and evidence guide:** 1) **Freedom and the New Nation: Federal, State, and Local Government.** 2) Federal. 3) New York State. 4) Local/city. 5) A level. 6) A branch job or government function. 7) Legislative, executive, judicial. 8) Congress, the legislative branch. 9) The president and executive branch. 10) Hear cases and explain/apply how laws apply. 11) Senate and Assembly. 12) Governor. 13) City/local. 14) 51. 15) Makes local laws or approves the city budget; accept either. 16) U.S. Department of State Passport Services; federal. 17) New York State DMV. 18) NYC311's DSNY collection-day/service information. 19) “Federal” identifies the level; “legislative” identifies a branch role. 20) Check the publisher, page heading, and specific service instructions; follow a link from an official agency page or contact the listed agency. Don't rely on a logo alone. For questions 13–18, answers should be checked against the linked official pages because government pages can change.

**Source and evidence notes:** The [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade) names Unit 4. [USAGov's branches page](https://www.usa.gov/branches-of-government) explains the federal branches. The [New York State Senate's branch overview](https://www.nysenate.gov/branches-government-new-york-state) describes the State Legislature, governor, and judiciary. The city's [Your Government page](https://www.nyc.gov/main/your-government) describes the Mayor and 51-member Council; the page returned an access block to the research fetcher during this pass, so re-open it in a regular browser before publishing or treat the cited city-role details as pending final page review. The [NYC311 collection information](https://portal.311.nyc.gov/article/?kanumber=KA-01801) points residents to DSNY schedules. [NY DMV renewal instructions](https://dmv.ny.gov/driver-license/renew-a-driver-license) are the state example. Social Studies.title: Social studies week: the Erie Canal — a route that changed New York
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** NYC Passport Grade 4 Unit 5 is **Making the Empire State: Immigration, Industrialization, and the Westward Movement**. This public-source week uses the Erie Canal as a case study within that unit. The NYC course page confirms the unit title, not P.S. 179's current lesson order. An older NYC materials list (2019–20) includes Patricia Drake's *New York's Erie Canal* among its Unit 5 books; that historical list does not prove the school still assigns that title. [NYCPS Grade 4 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade) · [NYCDOE 2019–20 Passport book list](https://infohub.nyced.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/grade-4-social-studies-curriculum.pdf).

**Reading — plain-English account from New York State, museum, and community sources:**

In the early 1800s, moving goods across New York could be slow and difficult. The New York State Canal Corporation explains that rough roads could become hard to use in summer or winter. A water route promised to connect the Hudson River and the Atlantic side of New York with Lake Erie and western places. In 1817, New York's legislature approved money to build the Erie Canal. The state authorized $7 million for a 363-mile waterway, about 40 feet wide. It opened in 1825 after eight years of construction. Those are the original canal figures in the state history; today's New York State Canal System has changed over time.

The original route ran from Albany toward Buffalo. A person studying an 1830 map can trace the Erie Canal and compare it with the railroads shown on the same map. Albany sits near the Hudson River; Buffalo sits at Lake Erie. Boats on the Erie could carry goods between western New York and the Hudson River route. From the Hudson, boats could continue south toward New York City and the Atlantic. A map shows a route; it does not, by itself, prove how every person felt about the canal.

Canals need a way to handle changes in water height. A **lock** is a water chamber with gates. A boat enters the chamber, the gates close, and water is added or let out until the water in the chamber is level with the water on the next part of the route. Then the far gate opens and the boat continues. This lets boats move through places where the canal changes height. The Erie Canal Museum's history describes locks as a key part of the canal system and notes that later enlargement projects changed the waterway and locks so larger boats could use them.

The canal helped some places grow, but its effects were not the same everywhere. An Erie Canal Museum account explains that Syracuse's salt industry used the canal to move salt; Rochester grew near the Genesee River's falls, where water power helped factories; and Lockport benefited from a set of locks. The same museum's exhibit describes Rome as a place the canal route bypassed, hurting its hoped-for connection and economy. So “the canal helped New York” is too broad to describe every town's experience. A stronger answer names a place and gives evidence for what happened there.

People's work and lives also belong in the story. One common claim says Irish immigrants built the original Erie Canal. An Erie Canal Museum educator explains that the claim is only partly right: Irish workers were numerous on later enlargement projects, while the original canal was built from 1817 to 1825. The canal museum also documents children, including immigrant and U.S.-born children, working on boats—walking animals on the towpath, helping on board, or doing other hard work. Do not turn this into a claim that every child had the same experience. The museum says some children lived with their boat-owning families and had schooling during the winter, while poorer children could face long hours and low pay.

The canal corridor had other, conflicting roles. New York State's Canal Corporation tells the story of Reverend Thomas James, who escaped enslavement by following the newly staked route west to Lockport and then crossing toward Canada. He later returned to New York and helped other freedom seekers. At the same time, canal traffic carried cotton produced by enslaved labor, as documented by the Erie Canal Museum. The waterway created routes for trade and communication, but it existed in a country where slavery and racist laws continued. A single “progress” story leaves out people who faced danger or harm.

The canal route also crossed Indigenous homelands. The Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor identifies the region as ancestral homelands of Haudenosaunee Nations and the Mohican Nation. The Oneida Nation's own history explains that New York State made many treaties between 1785 and 1846 through which it acquired most Oneida land. Those are two related facts from different sources; do not assume that a particular treaty was signed to build the canal unless a source says so. Grade 4's earlier Haudenosaunee unit is useful background. The communities are living Nations today, not only a subject from the past.

**Key words:** **canal** is a human-made waterway; **route** is a path from one place to another; **lock** is a gated water chamber that raises or lowers a boat; **trade** is buying, selling, or moving goods; **industrialization** is a change toward making more goods in factories; **immigrant** is a person who moves to a new country to live; **westward movement** is people moving toward western parts of the country; **evidence** is information that supports an answer; **perspective** is the point of view a source or person brings.

**Visual references:**

```text
LAKE ERIE / BUFFALO  →  west and central New York canal towns  →  ALBANY / HUDSON RIVER
                                                                          ↓
                                                             NEW YORK CITY / ATLANTIC

Lock model: boat enters chamber → gates close → water level changes → far gate opens
```

The route line is a guide-written locator, not a scale map. For map evidence, open the Library of Congress's [1830 map of U.S. canals and railroads](https://www.loc.gov/resource/g3701p.rr000010/); read its title and date, then zoom in on New York. It is five years after the canal opened, so it shows an early map of a working canal era, not a map from the planning stage. For today's geography, compare it with a current New York State Canal System map from [NYS Canals](https://www.canals.ny.gov/). Use the [Grade 4 source-analysis organizer](images/grade-04/social-studies/g04-social-source-analysis-organizer.png) to keep map observations separate from written-source explanations. No new AI image is required: the historical map and a simple student-drawn lock model are the right visuals for this evidence study.

**Five study sessions — about 50–65 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read the route map | Open the LOC 1830 map. Read its title/date and find Lake Erie, Buffalo, Albany, the Hudson River, and the canal line. Compare what a canal map includes with a map of today's state. | Draw a simple route map with a title, north arrow, named water bodies, and source line. Label it “not to scale.” Write one thing the map shows and one thing it cannot show. |
| 2 — Explain how a lock works | Reread the lock explanation. Draw a chamber with two gates, a boat, and high/low water levels. Act it out with a cup or two containers of water only if an adult can safely help; never use heavy objects or real waterways. | Write the steps in order: enter, close gates, change water level, open far gate, continue. Explain how a lock lets a boat move where the canal changes height. |
| 3 — Compare local effects | Read the Erie Canal Museum's examples of Syracuse, Rochester, Lockport, and Rome. For each place, make a “benefit / problem / source detail” card. Keep the town names attached to the claims. | Write a paragraph answering: “Did the canal help every town in the same way?” Use one supported example of a place that benefited and one of a place that was bypassed. |
| 4 — Study work and different experiences | Read the Canal Museum's child-labor note, the museum educator's correction about Irish workers, and the New York State Canal Corporation account of Thomas James. Add the Oneida and Canalway source notes about Indigenous homelands and land. | Make a four-row evidence table: immigrant workers, children, Black freedom seekers, Indigenous Nations. For each, write one source-supported fact and one question that source does not answer. Do not say one person's story describes a whole group. |
| 5 — Build a sourced museum panel | Revisit the 1830 map, the New York State Canal history, museum examples, and source notes. Complete the questions below. | Create a one-page museum panel called “The Erie Canal: a route with different effects.” Include the state decision and dates, a labeled map, one way a lock worked, two different town outcomes, and one paragraph about a worker or community perspective. Add source names and a sentence that limits what the evidence proves. |

**Evidence organizer:**

| Question | Best source to start with | Keep this distinction clear |
|---|---|---|
| What did New York State authorize, and when did the canal open? | NYS Canals history | State the original 1817 authorization and 1825 opening; do not mix original size with the modern canal system. |
| What does an 1830 map show? | Library of Congress map | It shows mapped routes and labels, not every shipment or person's view. |
| Which places benefited or were bypassed? | Erie Canal Museum's place examples | Name the community and source; do not assume all towns had one result. |
| Who worked or used the canal route? | Erie Canal Museum and NYS Canals “More Voices” | Do not repeat the simple “Irish built it” story without the museum's date distinction. |
| What happened to Indigenous land? | Erie Canalway acknowledgement and Oneida Nation history | The sources document homelands and state land-taking over time; do not claim a direct canal land deal without specific evidence. |

**Practice — guide-written questions, not copied from a school workbook:**

1. What is the full published title of NYC Passport Grade 4 Unit 5?
2. Which older NYC book list names *New York's Erie Canal*, and what year range does that list cover?
3. In which year did the New York State Legislature approve building the Erie Canal?
4. How much money did the state authorize for the original canal?
5. How long was the original Erie Canal, according to NYS Canals?
6. In what year did it open?
7. What two major water areas did the canal route connect, through Buffalo and Albany?
8. Why did New York seek a water route, according to the state history?
9. What does a lock do for a canal boat?
10. What is one thing the Library of Congress's 1830 map can show?
11. Why is the 1830 map not a map from before the canal was built?
12. Name one way the canal helped Syracuse, Rochester, or Lockport, according to the Erie Canal Museum account.
13. What does that account say happened to Rome in relation to the route?
14. Why is “the canal helped every town” too broad?
15. What correction does an Erie Canal Museum educator make to the claim that Irish immigrants built the original canal?
16. Give one type of work done by children on canal boats, according to the museum educator.
17. How did Thomas James use the canal's newly staked route when he escaped enslavement?
18. Name one way the canal corridor was connected to slavery or resistance to slavery.
19. What do the Erie Canalway and Oneida Nation sources together tell a reader about Indigenous land? What should the reader avoid claiming without more evidence?
20. Write a short museum-panel paragraph that uses two different sources to explain one benefit and one cost or unequal effect of the canal.

**Checked answers and evidence guide:** 1) **Making the Empire State: Immigration, Industrialization, and the Westward Movement.** 2) The NYC DOE Passport program materials list for school year **2019–20**; it lists *New York's Erie Canal* by Patricia Drake. It is an older inventory, not proof that a student currently uses that book. 3) 1817. 4) $7 million. 5) 363 miles. 6) 1825. 7) Lake Erie at Buffalo and the Hudson River at Albany (the Hudson route connects toward the Atlantic/New York City). 8) Roads could be slow and dangerous and difficult to use in different seasons; leaders sought a reliable way to move goods. 9) It changes the water level around a boat so it can move between higher and lower parts of the canal. 10) Accept mapped canals/railroads, routes, towns, or water features visible on the map. 11) It is dated 1830, after the canal's 1825 opening. 12) Accept Syracuse's salt industry using the canal to move salt; Rochester's factories using nearby water power; or Lockport benefiting from locks. 13) The museum account says the route bypassed Rome and hurt its hoped-for canal connection/economy. 14) Different towns had different route connections and effects; name evidence for each place. 15) The museum educator says Irish workers were especially numerous on later enlargement projects, not the original 1817–1825 construction period. 16) Walking/leading mules or horses, helping the cook, or another task listed by the educator. 17) He followed the newly marked route west to Lockport, then crossed toward Canada. 18) The canal corridor carried freedom seekers and abolitionist communication; it also carried cotton produced by enslaved labor. 19) The Canalway says the corridor crosses ancestral Haudenosaunee and Mohican homelands; the Oneida Nation says New York treaties from 1785–1846 transferred most Oneida lands to the state. Without a specific source, do not claim one treaty directly authorized the canal's route or that these Nations disappeared. 20) Check for two accurate facts from different linked sources, one benefit, one cost/unequal effect, and careful attribution. Accept original wording.

**Source and perspective notes:** The [NYCPS Grade 4 page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/4th-grade) supplies the current public Unit 5 title. The older [NYCDOE 2019–20 Passport inventory](https://infohub.nyced.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/grade-4-social-studies-curriculum.pdf) lists books for that program year. [New York State Canals' history](https://www.canals.ny.gov/About/History) supports the legislature's authorization, original length/width, and opening date. The [Library of Congress 1830 map](https://www.loc.gov/resource/g3701p.rr000010/) is a primary visual source for how canals and railroads were mapped after the canal opened. The [Erie Canal Museum's Erie Canal history](https://eriecanalmuseum.org/education/the-erie-canal/) provides canal dimensions and enlargement context; its [town-by-town exhibit](https://reflections.eriecanalmuseum.org/about/) describes Syracuse, Rochester, Lockport, and Rome. Its [child labor account](https://eriecanalmuseum.org/19th-century-kids-erie-canal/) explains the Irish-worker distinction and children's work. New York's [Canal Corporation More Voices account](https://www.canals.ny.gov/About/History/More-Voices) documents Thomas James and other African American histories. The [Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor](https://eriecanalway.org/learn/history-culture/native-americans) identifies Indigenous homelands along the corridor; the [Oneida Nation history](https://new.oneida-nsn.gov/pressroom/white-papers/) describes land transactions with New York State. These sources have different purposes and points of view; the lesson labels them rather than treating any one page as the whole story. This guide paraphrases public sources and does not reproduce a Passport workbook or the listed book.

Science.title: Science week: electric circuits and material tests
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Three circuit diagrams show a closed circuit with a lit bulb, an open switch with the bulb off, and an unknown material placed in a circuit gap](images/grade-04/science/g04-science-circuit-switch-test.png)

The third panel shows a material whose result has not been tested. Do not fill it with a guessed result. Record what happens in the actual classroom setup.

**Scope label:** New York Grade 4 science standards include energy transfer and circuits; this is a grade-level expectation, not evidence that Adnan or Manha's class is on this unit now. [NYS Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [NYCPS Grade 4 family overview](https://www.schools.nyc.gov/learning/student-journey/grade-by-grade/elementary-school-learning).

#### Learn it in plain English

A simple circuit has parts connected into a path. A classroom battery or cell supplies energy. Wires connect the parts. The bulb lights only when its two contacts are connected as the class kit requires and the path is closed. A switch can open the path or close it. If a wire is disconnected, there is a gap; the path is open and a correctly built classroom bulb should not light. If it does not light, check the whole setup before deciding why: the cell may be weak, the bulb may be loose, or a connection may be missing.

Some materials let current pass through the gap in a test circuit; these are called conductors in that setup. Other materials do not let enough current pass for the bulb to light; these are called insulators in that test. A result applies to the tested sample and setup. A coated, painted, wet, dirty, or unusually shaped sample may behave differently from a clean sample of the same base material. Do not claim every object made from a material will behave the same way after one test.

**Safe investigation:** use only the low-voltage classroom kit approved by the teacher/adult. Never connect wires or materials to a wall outlet. Do not test liquids, body parts, sharp objects, unknown powders, or anything the adult has not approved. Stop if a battery or wire becomes warm or damaged and tell the adult. Follow the kit directions.

To make a fair test, keep the battery, bulb, wires, and connection positions the same. Change only the sample placed in the gap. Before testing, write a prediction. After testing, write exactly what you observed. “The bulb lit” is an observation. “This sample completed the path in our setup” is a conclusion supported by that observation. If the bulb did not light, inspect the connections and repeat as directed before making a claim about the material.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Trace the path | Label cell, wires, bulb, and switch on the diagram. Trace the closed loop with a finger; mark the gap in the open-switch panel. Draw a circuit from the class model. | Explain which panel has a complete path and name the part that opens it. |
| 2 — Build a model safely | With adult guidance and the approved battery kit, assemble the class's closed circuit. Sketch actual connections before switching it on. Record the observed result without changing parts. | The drawing matches the real connection order and the observation describes what happened. |
| 3 — Open and close | Predict what will happen when the switch is opened. Change only the switch; observe, then close it and observe again. Record both trials. | State what changed and what stayed the same. Do not say the prediction was an observation. |
| 4 — Test one material | With adult-approved samples only, insert one sample into the gap. Keep all other parts fixed. Record sample, prediction, observed bulb result, and a cautious conclusion. Repeat only as the teacher directs. | A claim names the tested sample and setup; it does not generalize to every object. |
| 5 — Explain evidence | Review the records. Write a claim/evidence/reasoning paragraph. Include what you changed, what you saw, and one reason the result may need another trial. | Another student can tell which words are observations and which are conclusions. |

Use this record table in a notebook:

| Trial | Sample or switch setting | Prediction | What I observed | What the result suggests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Closed switch, no sample in gap |  |  |  |
| 2 | Open switch |  |  |  |
| 3 | Teacher-approved sample: ____ |  |  |  |

#### Practice set — new review questions, not school or NYSED test questions

1. Name the four main parts shown in the circuit image.
2. What does the switch do to the path when it is open?
3. In a working kit, a bulb does not light. Name two setup checks to make before blaming a material.
4. Why should a student change only one part during a fair test?
5. Is “the bulb lit” an observation or a conclusion?
6. Is “the sample let current pass in this setup” an observation or a conclusion?
7. A test bulb lights when sample A is placed in the gap. Write one careful claim and one claim that goes too far.
8. A student predicts the bulb will light but it stays dark. Which belongs in the results: the prediction or what was seen?
9. Why does one test not prove that every object made from the same material will behave the same way?
10. Name one unsafe action that this lesson forbids.
11. Draw a closed path and mark the place where the bulb's two contacts connect. Label the cell, wire, bulb, and switch.
12. Write a two-sentence claim/evidence response for a test you actually completed. If no test was completed, write a blank template instead of inventing an outcome.
