Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Cell/battery, wires, bulb, and switch.** Accept the labels used by the classroom kit.
2. It **breaks/opens the path**, so a correctly assembled bulb should not light while the switch is open.
3. Check that the cell is usable, the bulb is seated, and all wire contacts are connected as the kit directions show. Any two are acceptable.
4. Changing one part makes it possible to connect the observed difference to that change; changing several parts makes the cause unclear.
5. **Observation.** It reports what was directly seen.
6. **Conclusion.** It explains what the observation suggests about the sample in this particular setup.
7. Careful: “Sample A allowed the bulb to light in this test setup.” Too broad: “Every object made from this material always conducts.”
8. Record **what was seen**—the bulb stayed dark. Keep the prediction in its own column.
9. Different objects, coatings, shapes, contacts, or test setups can change the result; the test supports only a limited claim about the tested sample/setup.
10. Examples: using a wall outlet, testing a body part or liquid, or using an unapproved/unknown material. Never do these.
11. Answers vary. Credit a continuous connection that follows the approved kit diagram and labels all four parts; never connect to household electricity.
12. Answers depend on actual observations. A template may read: “I tested ____. I observed ____. This suggests ____ in this setup.” No result should be marked correct if it was invented.

**Mastery check:** the learner traces an open and closed path, follows the kit safety directions, makes a fair one-change test, separates prediction from observation, and limits conclusions to the evidence collected.

Science.title: Science week: water, wind, and changing land — weathering, erosion, and deposition
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Simplified model shows water and wind moving sediment and sand toward a place where a dune can collect](images/grade-04/science/g04-science-weathering-erosion-sediment.png)

**Scope label:** New York's Grade 4 standard 4-ESS2-1 asks students to use observations or measurements as evidence about weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation. This guide focuses its classroom investigation on water erosion. It is Grade 4 support, not proof that P.S. 179 has assigned this topic or follows this order. [New York State P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [NYCPS Grade 4 family overview](https://www.schools.nyc.gov/learning/student-journey/grade-by-grade/elementary-school-learning).

#### Learn it in plain English

Land can change slowly or quickly. **Weathering** breaks rock into smaller pieces where the rock is. **Erosion** moves rock pieces, soil, or sand from one place to another. **Deposition** happens when moving water or wind slows down and drops the material it was carrying. A piece can be weathered first, eroded later, and deposited somewhere else. These words describe different steps, so do not use them as if they mean the same thing.

Water can erode land when rain runs downhill. Moving water can pick up loose soil and carry it. Ice can crack rock as water freezes and expands in a crack. Wind can move dry sand. Plant roots can help hold soil in place, though plants do not prevent every kind of erosion. The New York standard asks students to investigate one form at a time so evidence has a clear focus.

#### Source reading: how the Great Sand Dunes formed

The Great Sand Dunes are in Colorado's San Luis Valley. The valley lies between the San Juan Mountains and the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The National Park Service describes a long story involving water, lakes, streams, sediment, and wind—not one storm or one simple cause.

Over a very long time, streams carried sediment, including sand, from the surrounding mountains into the valley. Lakes and wetlands sometimes covered parts of the valley. When water levels fell, sand could remain exposed. Winds then moved the exposed sand toward a bend in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The mountain passes and the shape of the valley helped direct the wind. Sand grains often bounce or roll along the ground instead of staying high in the air. During storms, winds can blow back toward the valley. The Park Service explains that these different wind directions help the dunes grow upward and make it harder for them to move into the mountains.

That history includes erosion and deposition: water and wind moved sediment, and sand collected in places where conditions let it settle. It also includes older changes to the valley and mountains. The Park Service says the full story is complex and continues to be studied. A classroom tray is only a model. It cannot reproduce the size, time, weather, rocks, plants, or many forces involved in the real landscape. [National Park Service: Geology of Great Sand Dunes](https://www.nps.gov/grsa/learn/nature/geology.htm).

**Read for evidence:** In a notebook, make three columns: *source fact*, *what process it supports*, and *what the source does not prove*. Record at least four details from the reading. For example, “Streams carried sand into the valley” is a source fact. It supports the idea that water moved sediment. It does not prove that water alone built the dunes.

#### Five study sessions — about 55–65 minutes each

| Session | Lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Sort the processes | Read “Learn it in plain English.” Draw three boxes labeled weathering, erosion, and deposition. Add the land-change action that defines each word. Sort six teacher-read examples. Explain why “a river carries sand” is movement, not settling. | Student can describe what happens to the material and whether it stays in place, moves, or settles. |
| 2 — Read the real landscape | Read the Great Sand Dunes source summary and open the National Park Service page. Find the valley, the two mountain ranges, streams, lakes/wetlands, and wind in the source. Build a sequence using only details the source gives. Mark any step that the source describes as a broad explanation rather than a complete account. | Sequence includes water bringing sediment, exposed sand, wind moving it, and sand collecting; student does not claim wind or water acted alone. |
| 3 — Plan a fair water test | Ask: “How does slope affect the amount of soil carried by water in our tray model?” Choose two or three slope settings. Keep soil type and amount, tray size, water volume, pour height, pour time, and collection cup the same. Decide how to measure collected sediment after it settles. Draw the setup and write the one variable that changes. | A partner can point to the changed variable and name at least three things held steady. |
| 4 — Test, measure, repeat | With an adult, place the same measured soil amount in the tray. Use the planned water amount and collection method. Repeat each slope setting three times if time and materials allow. Record actual observations, including spills or setup problems. Let the water settle before comparing sediment; do not invent or copy a result from another group. | Table contains real trial records, units, and a note about anything that made a trial unfair. |
| 5 — Explain evidence and limits | Compare repeated trials. State whether your results suggest a pattern in this model. Use at least two recorded measurements or observations. Explain one limitation and connect the work to the Great Sand Dunes reading. Finish the practice set. | Claim matches the group's records; student distinguishes the tray model from evidence about the real park. |

#### Investigation record

Use this blank table. Measure the collected sediment in the same way each time—for example, compare the settled layer using a ruler after the same wait time. If the class uses another measure, write the tool and unit. These measurements are not National Park Service data.

| Slope setting | Trial 1: actual measure | Trial 2: actual measure | Trial 3: actual measure | Notes about the setup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Low |  |  |  |  |
| Medium |  |  |  |  |
| Steep |  |  |  |  |

**Keep the test fair:** change only slope. Keep soil amount and kind, water amount, pour height and time, tray, and collection method the same. Use an adult-approved tray and clean water. Do not taste soil or water; wash hands afterward. Keep water away from electrical items. If the class cannot safely collect or measure runoff, use a teacher demonstration and record only what the class actually observes.

#### Practice — source study and new guide questions

Questions 1–6 use the National Park Service source reading above. Questions 7–13 are guide-created practice about the investigation; they are not school assignments, NYSED test items, or measurements from the park.

1. Name the two mountain ranges around the San Luis Valley named in the reading.
2. What did streams carry into the valley?
3. What could happen to sand when a lake or wetland's water level fell?
4. In the source reading, what moved the exposed sand toward the mountains?
5. Give one reason the dunes' formation cannot be explained by wind alone.
6. Which process word best describes sand settling after moving water slows: weathering, erosion, or deposition? Explain.
7. In the tray investigation, the question is about slope. Name the one variable to change and three conditions to keep the same.
8. Why should the class use the same amount of water for each slope setting?
9. A group records a larger settled sediment layer for one setting in two trials, but a smaller layer in the third. What should it do before making a strong claim?
10. A learner writes, “Our steep tray proves steep hills always erode more in nature.” Name two reasons this conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
11. The class gets 9 mm, 12 mm, and 9 mm in three repeats of one setting. What is the total? What is the mean (average)? Show the calculation.
12. A student says, “The soil broke into pieces, so that is erosion.” What question would help decide whether it was weathering or erosion?
13. Write a claim using two measurements from your actual table. If the investigation has not been done, leave the numbers blank and write a claim frame instead.

#### Visuals for the lesson

The source-based diagram is planned to show the sequence at a glance. Keep its arrows and labels simple and treat it as a model, not a map or a complete geological history. The written reading carries the full explanation and limitations.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer and evidence guide

1. The **San Juan Mountains** and the **Sangre de Cristo Mountains**.
2. Streams carried sediment, including sand, from the surrounding mountains into the valley.
3. Sand could be left exposed after the water level fell.
4. **Wind** moved exposed sand toward a bend in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.
5. The source describes water carrying sediment, lakes and wetlands exposing sand, the shape of the valley and mountain passes, and winds from different directions. Any one or more of these supports the answer.
6. **Deposition**, because the moving material settles or is dropped after the water slows. Erosion describes the movement before it settles.
7. Change the **slope**. Keep the soil kind and amount, water volume, pour height/time, tray, and collection method the same. Any three steady conditions are acceptable.
8. If water volume changes too, the class cannot tell whether a difference came from slope or from the extra or reduced water. A fair comparison changes one planned factor.
9. Check for spills, uneven soil, a different pour, or another setup change; repeat the setting under the same conditions if possible. Report all trials and uncertainty rather than hiding the different result.
10. The tray is a small model, and one soil type or water method does not represent every hillside. The class's trials also measure only the tested slope settings and conditions; they do not prove what always happens in nature.
11. Total: **9 + 12 + 9 = 30 mm**. Mean: **30 ÷ 3 = 10 mm**.
12. Ask: **Did the pieces stay where they broke, or were they carried to a different place?** Breaking in place is weathering; moving material is erosion.
13. Answers must match the student's own recorded measurements. Accept: “In our tray model, the ____ slope setting had ____ mm of settled sediment in trial __ and ____ mm in trial __. This suggests __ under our test conditions.” If no test was run, the blanks stay blank; no result may be made up.

**Mastery check:** the learner can tell weathering, erosion, and deposition apart; pull accurate facts from the park source; plan a one-variable comparison; record actual measurements with units; and state what the model cannot prove.

Science.title: Science week: bird beaks as structures that help birds get food
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Grade-level scope:** New York Grade 4 science expectation 4-LS1-1 asks students to use evidence to explain how plant and animal structures support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction. It limits assessment to structures large enough to observe. This week studies a bird's beak as an external structure. It is grade-level support, not a claim about P.S. 179's current unit or assigned textbook. [New York State Grades 3–5 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/3-5-science-learning-standards.pdf).

**Real source and classroom activity:** The National Park Service publishes a fourth-grade **Bird Beak Adaptations** lesson about Zion's birds and an activity in which students model feeding with different beak shapes. Its separate **Bird Beak Buffet** activity gives the utensil, food-item, timer, and observation steps used below. These are public NPS learning resources, not P.S. 179 materials. [NPS Bird Beak Adaptations lesson](https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/bird-beak-adaptations.htm); [NPS Bird Beak Buffet activity](https://www.nps.gov/articles/birdbeakbuffet.htm).

![A Hawaiian stilt and a coot forage in a fishpond](https://www.nps.gov/puho/images/bird-beaks.jpg)

*NPS photo of real birds for comparison with the model. Look closely at the visible bills; do not infer the birds' full diet from this one image. [Image and activity source: National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/articles/birdbeakbuffet.htm).*

#### Source reading: model a beak, then check what the model can tell you

The National Park Service says Zion National Park is home to more than 200 bird species. Birds have feathers and wings, and they have a beak or bill. The NPS lesson explains that birds use the bill for several purposes, mainly to find and get food. Different bills can be studied as structures: their shape is something a learner can observe, and their use is something a learner should support with evidence. A photograph can show a bill's visible shape, but it does not show every action the bird can do or every food it eats. [NPS Bird Beak Adaptations lesson](https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/bird-beak-adaptations.htm).

In the NPS **Bird Beak Buffet**, a student uses a soup spoon, tweezers, or chopsticks to stand in for a beak. A cup stands in for a bird's stomach. The NPS activity lists pennies as clams, rice grains as small insects, rubber bands as worms, and pasta shells as beetles. These objects are models: they represent food for the game. They are not real bird food, and the game is not a test with live birds.

The NPS instructions say to scatter the food, use only the chosen utensil to pick it up, and stop after 20 seconds. The player records which “bill” was used and how many of each kind of model food reached the cup. Then the player repeats with a different bill and may test one food kind at a time or all kinds together. The student can compare what happened in the model. The result does not prove that a real bird would choose the same food or survive better. To explain a real bird, use information about that species and its surroundings from a reliable source.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read and observe | Read the source passage and open both NPS pages. In the photograph, identify the visible beaks and write two details you can actually see. In a second column, list questions the photo cannot answer. Mark each statement as a source fact, a visible observation, or a question. | Student can name a beak as an external structure and does not claim the photograph proves a complete diet. |
| 2 — Plan the model | Review the NPS materials and directions. Choose three safe utensil “bills.” For a small-parts-safe version, an adult may replace the tiny rice and loose food items with larger washable counters while keeping the same kind and number in every comparison; record the change. Predict which utensil will collect a chosen model food most easily, and label this as a prediction. | Model key names what each utensil, food item, and cup represents. Prediction is separate from a measured result. |
| 3 — Run controlled rounds | With adult oversight, select one model food type. Scatter the same number of items in the same area. #### Checked answer and evidence guide

1. **4-LS1-1**, about using evidence to explain how plant and animal structures support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.
2. A utensil represents a bird's **beak or bill**.
3. The cup represents the bird's **stomach** in the model.
4. **Soup spoon, tweezers, and chopsticks.**
5. **Pennies = clams; rice grains = small insects; rubber bands = worms; pasta shells = beetles.** These are the game's representations, not actual food placed before birds.
6. **20 seconds.**
7. The student records which bill/utensil was used and the number of each kind of model food in the cup.
8. It keeps the rule consistent so the comparison tests the utensil model; hands or cup-scooping would add another way to collect food.
9. Keep the food type, starting number of pieces, scatter area, time, and collection rules the same. Any four are acceptable.
10. A **prediction**; it states what the student expects before measuring.
11. A **source fact** about what the NPS instructions say. It is not a result from the student's own trial.
12. Add the three actual counts to find the **total**. Divide that total by **3** to find the **mean per trial**. The numeric answer depends on the student's recorded data.
13. **Answers vary with actual results.** The learner should compare the recorded counts for the same model food and state only the pattern the table supports. If no activity was done, leave the result blank and write a claim frame; do not invent data.
14. NPS says birds mainly use the bill to **forage for and obtain food**.
15. Example observation: **the photo shows visible bills and birds foraging.** It cannot by itself prove every food they eat, how often they eat it, or how a bill performs in every setting.
16. **No.** The utensil is only a model. It does not copy a bird's full body, behavior, habitat, or real food, and the trial uses human-made rules and objects.
17. Two things changed, so the count difference could be caused by the utensil, the food, or both. Change one planned factor at a time.
18. **Answers vary.** The claim must match actual evidence. Example frame: “The NPS source says ____. In my model, I observed ____. This supports the idea that ____, but the model cannot show ____ about a living bird.” Accept source facts from the linked NPS pages and actual, accurately reported trial data.

Math.explanation: To round a number to the nearest ten thousand, locate the two neighboring ten-thousands. Find the halfway point between them. A number below the halfway point rounds down; a number at or above it rounds up. For 224,830, the neighbors are 220,000 and 230,000. The halfway point is 225,000, and 224,830 is below it, so the number rounds to 220,000.

## Science

No current P.S. 179 Grade 4 science textbook/unit map was found publicly. NYS Grade 4 standards cover:

- **Energy and electricity:** energy transfer/conversion, circuits, and how energy can produce motion, sound, heat, or light.
- **Waves, light, and information:** light travels and interacts with objects; patterns can carry information.
- **Structures and functions of organisms:** how structures support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.
- **Earth features and processes:** patterns in rocks, landforms, and Earth materials provide evidence of change over time.
- **Natural resources and human effects:** use evidence to describe how people can affect the environment and how design can reduce impacts.

These are NYS standards topics, not an assertion that these are the next P.S. 179 lessons. [NYS P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); NYC’s grade overview gives a family-facing summary of Grade 4 science and history topics [here](https://www.schools.nyc.gov/learning/student-journey/grade-by-grade/elementary-school-learning).

### How to study these science topics from evidence

For **circuits**, record which components are connected and whether a bulb lights; use the NYS performance expectation to explain the evidence, rather than memorizing an unsupported “electricity flows” picture. For **light**, compare what happens when light meets transparent, translucent, and opaque materials. For **landforms**, compare maps, rock/soil observations, or dated images to identify evidence of change. These are study approaches aligned to the cited state standards, not claims about the materials P.S. 179 uses.
